label: Retention schedules, disposal and the hold that overrides both

mentor.diagnosis: You treated retention as a storage decision. A retention schedule says both how long you must keep data and when you must stop keeping it, and a legal hold overrides the second half.
contrast: Keep for a defined minimum, usually set by law or contract
Destroy or sanitise once the period expires
Keeping it forever is a liability, not prudence
Preserve everything relevant, suspending normal deletion
Automated deletion continuing during litigation is spoliation
Retiring the asset itself: remove from service, from inventory, from access
A forgotten server still running, unpatched and unmonitored
Documented evidence that media was sanitised or destroyed
No proof, so the obligation is unmet even if the work was done
mentor.rule: Retention sets a floor and a ceiling. Data kept past the ceiling is pure liability, and a legal hold is the one thing that lifts the ceiling.
mentor.tell: Litigation or an investigation in progress points to legal hold. An expired period with data still present points to a disposal failure.
mentor.trap: Keeping everything indefinitely feels safe and is not. Data you no longer need is still discoverable, still breachable and still your responsibility.

mentor.diagnosis: You named a stage of the asset lifecycle that does not match where the failure happened. The lifecycle is procurement, assignment, tracking, disposal, and each has its own failure.
contrast: Buying something that cannot meet policy
A named owner and a classification
Nobody accountable when a decision is needed
A current inventory of what exists
Defending an estate you cannot enumerate
Data destroyed, asset removed from the register
A sold laptop carrying readable company data
mentor.rule: You cannot secure, patch, or decommission an asset you do not know you own. The inventory is the control everything else depends on.
mentor.tell: 'Devices were found running unsupported software nobody knew existed' is an inventory and tracking failure, before it is a patching one.
mentor.trap: Patching is the instinctive answer to anything about out-of-date systems. You cannot patch what is not in the inventory, which is why asset management sits underneath vulnerability management.

mentor.diagnosis: You chose a disposal method that does not match whether the asset is being reused, and you may have skipped the evidence step.
contrast: The device is being redeployed, sold or returned on lease
The data is too sensitive to risk, or the media has failed
Always, when a third party did the work or an auditor will ask
mentor.rule: Reuse means sanitize. No reuse and high sensitivity means destroy. Either way, get the certificate, because without it you cannot prove it happened.
mentor.tell: 'The drives were sent to a disposal vendor' should make you look for certification. The control is not complete without evidence.
mentor.trap: Degaussing is a destruction method for magnetic media and does nothing to an SSD, which stores no magnetic domains. Media type decides which destruction method is real.
